q: Your checkout service latency doubles every day at exactly 14:00 and recovers by itself an hour later. How do you find out why?
sym: p99 latency of checkout doubles daily from 14:00 to 15:00, then recovers with no human action. No deploys at that time.
inv: # line up the window with scheduled work
# compare dependency latencies in that window
# check traffic mix and batch jobs on the DB
select query, calls from pg_stat_statements order by total_exec_time desc limit 5
cause: A daily analytics export job starts at 14:00 on the primary database and competes for IO and locks with checkout queries.
fix: # move the export to a read replica
pg_dump --host replica ...
# or reschedule to off-peak and throttle IO
ionice -c3 nice -n19 ./export.sh
prev: Inventory scheduled jobs per shared resource, run heavy reads on replicas, and add a latency SLO alert with a time-pattern annotation.
tip: Anything that repeats on a clock is a schedule. Look for cron, batch, certificate or cache expiry before suspecting code.
a: A problem that begins at exactly the same time every day and fixes itself points to something scheduled, not a code bug. I first overlay the latency window on everything that runs on a clock: cron jobs and Kubernetes cron jobs, backups, analytics exports, cache or token expiry, and partner traffic that is time-zone based. Then I look at which dependency's latency rises at the same moment, and at the database's top queries and lock waits during the window versus outside it. In this case I find a daily export running on the primary, competing for disk and locks with checkout transactions. The fix is moving the job to a read replica or off-peak, and throttling it with lower IO priority. To prevent recurrence, I keep an inventory of scheduled jobs against shared resources, enforce that heavy reads use replicas, and annotate dashboards with job schedules so a repeating pattern is recognised immediately.
f: What else repeats on a clock?
Why use a read replica?

q: One customer reports errors but your dashboards show a 99.99% success rate. How do you investigate a single-tenant problem?
sym: A single large customer sees failures. Global error rate is normal. Support has a request ID or tenant ID.
inv: grep tenant_id=acme app.log | grep -i error | tail
# compare config, data size and quotas for that tenant
select count(*) from orders where tenant_id='acme'
cause: The tenant has a data volume 50x the median, so a query with no index on that tenant partition times out only for them.
fix: # immediate: raise timeout or add index concurrently
create index concurrently on orders (tenant_id, created_at);
# route their traffic to a larger pool if needed
prev: Track SLIs per tenant tier, alert on outliers, load test with whale-sized tenants, and add per-tenant query budgets.
tip: Averages hide the biggest customers. Always be able to slice by tenant, region and version.
a: Global success rate is dominated by the majority of traffic, so a single big tenant can be completely broken without moving it. I start by slicing metrics, logs and traces by tenant to confirm the pattern, then find their failed requests using the request or tenant ID. I compare what is different about them: data volume, features enabled, rate limits and quotas, region, client version and configuration. Often the answer is scale, such as a data set fifty times the median, so a query that is fine for others times out for them. I mitigate with a targeted fix, for example adding an index, increasing the timeout for that route or moving the tenant to bigger capacity, and keep the customer informed. For prevention, I add per-tenant SLIs for the largest customers, test with realistic whale-sized data, and set per-tenant query budgets and alerts for outliers so I see it before they call.
f: Why slice by tenant?
What is a whale tenant?

q: An incident is resolved, but the same alert returns three times the next day with a different apparent cause each time. What is going on?
sym: Repeat incidents, each blamed on a different cause, each 'fixed' individually. The alert keeps returning.
inv: # build a combined timeline of all four occurrences
# look for a common precursor: change, load, resource
# check shared resources: connection pool, node, queue
show max_connections; select count(*) from pg_stat_activity;
cause: A shared resource (connection pool) is near its limit, so any minor trigger tips it over. The 'different causes' were just different triggers.
fix: # raise and right-size the pool, add pgbouncer
# add saturation alert at 80% pool use
# fix the leaking client that never returns connections
prev: Alert on saturation, not just failures; after repeated incidents, look for a common underlying constraint instead of treating each trigger separately.
tip: When causes keep changing, you are probably fixing triggers. Look for the shared constraint that makes the system fragile.
a: If the same symptom recurs with a new explanation every time, I suspect we are treating triggers and missing the underlying fragility. I build one timeline across all occurrences and look for what they share: a resource near its limit, a common dependency, a time pattern, or a recent change that altered a margin. For example, a database connection pool running at ninety-five percent has no slack, so a small traffic increase, a slow query or a deployment can each push it over, and each looks like a different cause. I confirm with saturation metrics at the time of each incident, then fix the constraint: resize the pool, introduce a pooler, find the leak that holds connections, and add an alert on saturation so I get warned before failure. I also record in the postmortem that the individual triggers were symptoms, and track recurrence so the problem is addressed systematically.
f: Why look for shared constraints?
What alert catches this earlier?

q: You are on call and two unrelated alerts fire at the same time on different services. How do you prioritise?
sym: Alert A: payments error rate rising. Alert B: internal reporting job failing. Only one on-call.
inv: check SLO burn and customer-facing impact for each
# are they related? shared dependency or change?
git log --since='30 min ago'; check shared DB/queue health
page secondary, declare incident for the highest-impact
cause: They were unrelated: payments degradation from a provider issue, reporting failure from an expired credential.
fix: # payments first: failover to secondary provider
# ask secondary on-call to take reporting
# log reporting as ticket with owner and ETA
prev: Define severities, keep a secondary on-call, and tag alerts with business impact so triage is quick under pressure.
tip: Triage by user and business impact, not by who shouted first. Delegate early.
a: With two alerts, I rank them by user and business impact and urgency. Payments errors affect revenue and customers now, while a failing internal report can usually wait unless it feeds a regulatory deadline. I quickly check whether the two are related, looking at recent changes and shared dependencies, because a common cause changes the approach. I then act on the most severe one, declare an incident if needed, and bring in help: I page the secondary on-call or another team to handle the second alert so I am not context-switching. The less severe item is acknowledged, with a note of its status and an owner, so it is not lost. I communicate the priorities in the incident channel so stakeholders know what is happening. Later I check that severities and routing were right, and adjust alert metadata for faster triage.
f: How do you rank alerts?
When do you declare an incident?

q: A new engineer deployed a hotfix directly to production, bypassing the pipeline, and now things are inconsistent. How do you recover and fix the process?
sym: Manual change on some servers only. Behaviour differs per host. Git and prod no longer match.
cause: A manual binary swap on three of ten hosts left mixed versions, and the change never went through review or tests.
fix: # bring all hosts back to the pipeline-built version
./deploy.sh --version 2026.10.3 --all
# add the hotfix properly via PR + CI
# document the change in the incident log
prev: Remove direct prod write access, provide a fast hotfix lane in the pipeline, use immutable infrastructure, and treat the event as a systems problem, not a personal one.
tip: People bypass the pipeline when it is slow or when they do not trust it. Make the right way the fast way.
a: My first step is to establish what is running where: compare versions or file hashes across hosts and check the audit log for who changed what, so I understand the drift. To recover, I redeploy a known version from the pipeline to every host so all are consistent, and then submit the hotfix as a proper change through code review and tests so it is tracked and repeatable. I talk to the engineer without blame to understand why they bypassed the pipeline: was it too slow in an emergency, did they lack access to a hotfix path, or did nobody explain? The systemic fixes are removing direct write access to production, creating an expedited hotfix lane with essential checks, using immutable deployments so manual edits are impossible or detected, and drift detection that alerts when running state differs from the declared one. Training and onboarding then reinforce the process.
f: Why avoid blaming the engineer?
How do you detect drift?

q: A customer-facing feature breaks only when a specific third-party script or ad blocker is present. How do you diagnose a client-side issue from the server side?
sym: Support reports a page blank for some users. Server logs are clean, API returns 200.
inv: filter JS errors by browser, extension, URL
# reproduce with the same browser profile
# compare requests with and without the extension
cause: A blocking extension blocks a first-party analytics script whose failure throws an unhandled exception that halts rendering.
fix: # wrap analytics init in try/catch, load async
# deploy frontend fix, verify via RUM error rate
prev: Treat third-party scripts as untrusted, load them non-blocking, add RUM error tracking and synthetic checks across browsers.
tip: Server-side 200s do not mean the user's page works. You need real user monitoring.
a: When server logs and dashboards look clean but users see a broken page, the problem is likely in the browser. I check real user monitoring and client error reports, filtering by browser, version and extension patterns, and look for the common factor among affected users. Then I reproduce with the same environment, for example a browser with the blocker enabled, and watch the console and network tab. Here the blocker prevents an analytics script loading, and the page's code assumed it exists and threw an unhandled exception, stopping rendering. The fix is defensive: wrap third-party initialisation in error handling, load such scripts asynchronously so they cannot block the page, and deploy the frontend update, verifying with the client error rate. For prevention, I include real user monitoring and error tracking in the standard stack, add synthetic checks with several browsers, and treat third-party scripts as unreliable dependencies.
f: Why is RUM needed?
How should third-party scripts be loaded?

q: The database is healthy and the app is healthy, but a specific API endpoint returns 504 after exactly 30 seconds. Where do you look?
sym: 504 Gateway Timeout on one endpoint at exactly 30s. Other endpoints fine.
inv: # a round number means a configured timeout
kubectl get ingress api -o yaml | grep -i timeout
# find the slow step inside that endpoint
trace the request; check outbound calls and locks
cause: The endpoint calls a slow report generator that takes 45s; the load balancer idle timeout of 30s cuts it before the app finishes.
fix: # short term: raise LB/ingress timeout for that route
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "60"
# real fix: make it async with a job id and polling
prev: Set timeouts consistently across layers, keep synchronous requests short, and design long operations as asynchronous jobs.
tip: Exact round-number durations almost always mean a timeout setting somewhere in the path.
a: A failure at exactly thirty seconds is a signature of a configured timeout rather than random slowness. I list every layer between the client and the code, the CDN, load balancer, ingress, proxy, application server and client library, and find which has a thirty second limit. Then I trace the endpoint to see why it takes longer than that: here it generates a report that needs forty-five seconds. The quick mitigation is raising the timeout on that route at the ingress and load balancer, keeping the layers' timeouts ordered so that the inner ones expire before the outer ones. The proper fix is redesigning the operation to be asynchronous: the request starts a job and returns an identifier immediately, the client polls or receives a notification. Prevention includes documenting timeouts across layers, alerting on requests near the limit, and discouraging long synchronous operations in API design.
f: Why do round numbers matter?
Why make long operations async?

q: After a datacenter power event all servers came back, but some services are in a bad state. In what order do you bring things back and verify?
sym: Mass restart after power loss. Services started in random order, some failing on missing dependencies.
inv: 1. network, DNS, NTP  2. storage/DB/queues  3. identity/secrets  4. core services  5. edge/LB
# verify each layer before the next
systemctl --failed; kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running
cause: Services started before DNS and the database quorum were ready and cached failures; the database had a stale replica.
fix: # restart in dependency order, validate each tier
# resync stale replica from primary
# restart services that cached bad state
prev: Document and automate startup ordering, add readiness gates and retries with backoff, test cold-start recovery in drills.
tip: Bring up foundation services first and verify each layer. Starting everything at once creates cascading confusion.
a: After a mass restart, I avoid starting everything at once. I work bottom-up through the dependency layers: first the network, DNS and time synchronisation, because many things fail strangely without them; then storage, databases and message queues, verifying file system checks, cluster quorum and replication status; then identity and secrets services; then the core application services; and finally edge components like load balancers and caches. At each layer I confirm health before moving on. Services that started too early and cached failures, such as an empty DNS answer, get restarted. I check data integrity carefully, particularly any replica that may be stale or corrupted, and resynchronise it from the primary if necessary. Afterwards I run synthetic end-to-end checks. To prevent chaos next time, I document and automate the startup order, build readiness checks and retries with backoff into services, and practise cold-start drills.
f: What starts first?
Why restart services that cached failures?

q: A Deployment shows all pods Running but the Service has no endpoints. How do you debug it?
sym: kubectl get pods shows Running, but requests to the Service fail with connection refused. kubectl get endpoints shows none.
inv: kubectl get svc api -o yaml | grep -A3 selector
cause: The Service selector uses app=api but pods are labelled app=api-v2, or the pods are Running but not Ready because the readiness probe fails.
fix: # fix labels or selector
kubectl patch svc api -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"api-v2"}}}'
# or fix the readiness probe path/port
kubectl rollout status deploy/api
prev: Use Helm templates that derive selectors and labels from one helper, and add a post-deploy check that endpoints are non-empty.
tip: Endpoints only include pods that are Ready and match the selector. Check both conditions.
a: A Service routes to endpoints, which Kubernetes builds from pods that match the selector and are Ready. If the endpoint list is empty while pods are running, one of those two conditions fails. I compare the Service selector with the pod labels using show-labels; a typo or a changed label after a refactor is very common. If the labels match, I check readiness: describe the pod to see whether the readiness probe is failing, for instance because the path, port or required dependency is wrong, which keeps the pod out of the endpoints even though the container runs. I also check that the target port matches the container port and that the namespace is correct. The fix is correcting the selector or the probe, then verifying that the endpoints appear. To prevent this, I generate labels and selectors from shared templates and add a deployment check that endpoints are not empty.
f: What makes a pod appear in endpoints?
How do you verify the fix?

q: A StatefulSet pod won't start because its PersistentVolumeClaim is bound to a volume in a different availability zone. What happened and how do you fix it?
sym: Pod Pending with 'volume node affinity conflict' or 'had volume node affinity conflict'.
inv: kubectl get pv <name> -o yaml | grep -A8 nodeAffinity
cause: The EBS volume lives in zone a, but the only schedulable nodes (due to capacity or taints) are in zone b; block volumes cannot cross zones.
fix: # add capacity in zone a
# or restore from snapshot into zone b
aws ec2 create-volume --snapshot-id snap-123 --availability-zone eu-west-1b
# use volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
prev: Use WaitForFirstConsumer storage classes, spread node groups per zone, and keep topology spread constraints and capacity in every zone.
tip: Block storage is zonal. Scheduling must follow the data, not the other way around.
a: Block volumes such as EBS exist in a single availability zone and can only attach to nodes in that zone. The pod's claim is already bound to a volume in zone a, so the scheduler may only place the pod on nodes in zone a. If there are none with enough capacity, or they are cordoned or tainted, the pod stays pending with a node affinity conflict. The quick fix is to restore capacity in zone a: scale that node group, remove the blocking taint, or free resources. If zone a is unavailable, I can restore the data from a snapshot into a new volume in another zone and recreate the claim. Longer term, I configure the storage class with wait-for-first-consumer binding so volumes are created in the zone where the pod is scheduled, maintain node groups in every zone with enough headroom, and consider replication at the application layer so the loss of one zone is survivable.
f: Why can't volumes cross zones?
What does WaitForFirstConsumer do?

q: After upgrading the cluster, many pods fail with 'no matches for kind' or deprecated API errors during deploy. How do you recover and prevent this?
sym: kubectl apply fails: 'no matches for kind Ingress in version extensions/v1beta1'. Helm releases cannot upgrade.
cause: Manifests and Helm release history reference API versions removed in the new Kubernetes version.
fix: # update manifests to supported API versions
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
helm mapkubeapis myrelease
# redeploy and verify
prev: Scan for deprecated APIs before every upgrade, read release notes, test upgrades in staging and keep charts current.
tip: Deprecated APIs are announced many releases ahead. Scanners such as pluto or kubent find them in minutes.
a: Kubernetes removes deprecated API versions on a published schedule, and manifests or stored Helm release data that still use them break after an upgrade. To recover, I identify which resources use removed versions, using the API server's deprecated request metrics and static scanners like pluto against manifests and Helm releases. I update manifests to the supported versions, for example the stable networking API for ingress, and for existing Helm releases I use the map-deprecated-APIs plugin to rewrite stored release manifests so that upgrades work. Then I redeploy and validate that workloads are healthy. To prevent it, my upgrade process includes scanning for deprecated and soon-to-be-removed APIs before upgrading, reading release notes, upgrading a staging cluster first with the real manifests, and keeping charts and operators updated. I also monitor the deprecated API usage metric continuously, not only at upgrade time.
f: How do you find deprecated APIs?
Why test upgrades in staging first?

q: Your cluster DNS (CoreDNS) is overloaded and pods see intermittent 'no such host' errors under load. What do you check and change?
sym: Random resolution failures and slow lookups, especially during traffic peaks. CoreDNS pods at high CPU.
inv: kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml
cause: ndots:5 makes every external lookup try multiple search domains first, multiplying queries; CoreDNS has too few replicas and no node-local cache.
fix: # lower ndots or use FQDNs with trailing dot
dnsConfig: options: [{name: ndots, value: "2"}]
kubectl scale deploy coredns -n kube-system --replicas=6
# deploy NodeLocal DNSCache
prev: Run node-local DNS caching, autoscale CoreDNS with cluster-proportional-autoscaler, and monitor DNS latency and error rate.
tip: With ndots 5, one lookup for api.example.com can generate five or more queries. Use trailing dots for external names.
a: DNS problems in Kubernetes under load often come from query amplification and insufficient capacity. By default pods have the ndots option set to five, so a name with fewer than five dots, such as api.example.com, is first tried with each search domain appended, producing several failed queries before the correct one, and in a busy cluster that multiplies traffic onto CoreDNS. I check CoreDNS CPU and logs, replica count, and the resolv.conf of the application pods. Mitigations are lowering ndots for workloads that mostly query external names, or using fully qualified names with a trailing dot, scaling the CoreDNS replicas, and deploying node-local DNS caching so most queries are answered on the node without crossing the network. I add autoscaling for CoreDNS proportional to cluster size, and monitoring for query rate, latency and SERVFAIL responses, so I see saturation before users see failures.
f: What does ndots do?
What is NodeLocal DNSCache?

q: A PodDisruptionBudget blocks a node drain during a cluster upgrade and the upgrade hangs. How do you handle it safely?
sym: kubectl drain waits forever: 'Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget.'
inv: kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=api -o wide
cause: PDB requires minAvailable 2 but the deployment has only 2 replicas, or an unhealthy pod already uses up the budget, so no pod can be evicted.
fix: # scale up temporarily so eviction is allowed
kubectl scale deploy/api --replicas=4
# fix the unhealthy replica
# long term: maxUnavailable: 1 with enough replicas
prev: Set PDBs relative to replica counts, never minAvailable equal to replicas, and test drains in staging before production upgrades.
tip: A PDB that allows zero disruptions makes the node undrainable. Check allowedDisruptions.
a: A PodDisruptionBudget protects availability by limiting voluntary evictions, but a badly set one can block maintenance. Describing the PDB shows how many disruptions are currently allowed. If minimum available equals the replica count, or one pod is already unhealthy, the allowed disruptions are zero and drain waits indefinitely. The safe response is not to force-delete pods, which would defeat the protection and might cause an outage. Instead I increase the replica count temporarily so that evicting one pod keeps the minimum, or fix the unhealthy pod so the budget recovers, then continue the drain. I never bypass the budget on a critical service without agreement. For the long term, I define PDBs using max unavailable of one, ensure at least two or three replicas for critical services, and include drain tests in the upgrade checklist, so these conflicts are discovered before the maintenance window.
f: What is allowedDisruptions?
Why not delete the pods directly?

q: Ingress returns 502 for a few seconds after every deployment, even with rolling updates. What causes it and what do you fix?
sym: Short bursts of 502/503 on each rollout, then normal. Readiness probes pass.
inv: kubectl get deploy api -o yaml | grep -A8 strategy
kubectl get deploy api -o yaml | grep -B2 -A10 lifecycle
# do old pods get SIGTERM before endpoints are removed?
cause: Pods receive SIGTERM and exit immediately while the ingress still routes to them, because endpoint removal propagates asynchronously.
fix: lifecycle: preStop: exec: command: ["sleep","15"]
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
# app: stop accepting new connections after SIGTERM, drain in-flight
maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 25%
prev: Standardise graceful shutdown in base charts, test rollouts under load in CI and monitor 5xx during deployments.
tip: Endpoint removal and SIGTERM race each other. A preStop sleep gives the proxies time to update.
a: The pattern is a short error burst at each rollout, which means that old pods are going away while traffic is still being sent to them. When Kubernetes terminates a pod, it removes it from endpoints and sends a termination signal at the same time, but the ingress controller and load balancers learn about the endpoint change a bit later. If the application exits immediately on the signal, requests in that window fail. The fix has several parts: add a pre-stop sleep of a few seconds so the pod keeps serving while the removal propagates, make the app handle the signal by stopping new connections and finishing in-flight requests, set the termination grace period to cover that, and configure the rolling update with no unavailable pods and some surge so capacity stays. I validate by running a load test during a rollout and checking that the error rate stays flat, and bake the settings into the base chart.
f: Why a preStop sleep?
How do you test the fix?

q: A namespace hits its ResourceQuota and new deployments fail with 'exceeded quota'. How do you resolve it without breaking other teams?
sym: Pods not created: forbidden: exceeded quota: requests.cpu. ReplicaSet events show failures.
cause: Over-requested CPU on idle services consumes the quota; real usage is a fraction of requests.
fix: # right-size requests using VPA recommendations
# remove unused workloads
# if justified, raise quota through the capacity process
prev: Review requests regularly, use VPA in recommendation mode, set LimitRanges with sensible defaults and track quota utilisation.
tip: Quota counts requests, not usage. Inflated requests waste shared cluster capacity.
a: Resource quotas limit the total requests and limits a namespace can claim, and pods that would exceed it are rejected at creation. I look at quota consumption against actual usage. A common situation is that teams copy generous requests into every service, so the sum of requests hits the quota while real usage is far lower. The first fix is to right-size: use observed usage and vertical autoscaler recommendations to lower requests on over-provisioned workloads, delete unused deployments and old jobs. If the team really needs more capacity, they raise a request through the capacity planning process, so the cluster has enough nodes. I avoid simply increasing the quota without checking the cluster headroom, as that can starve other teams. To prevent recurrence, I add default requests through limit ranges, dashboards showing requests versus usage per namespace, and a periodic review.
f: Do quotas count usage or requests?
What does a LimitRange do?

q: A critical controller or operator pod keeps getting evicted and restarted because the node is under memory pressure. How do you protect system-critical pods?
sym: Operator pod evicted repeatedly; custom resources stop reconciling; node condition MemoryPressure true.
inv: kubectl describe node n1 | grep -A8 Conditions
cause: The operator runs as BestEffort with no requests, so it is the first to be evicted when memory is short.
fix: # set requests=limits for Guaranteed QoS
resources: requests: {cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi} limits: {cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi}
priorityClassName: system-cluster-critical
# fix the noisy neighbours without limits
prev: Require resource requests on all workloads, use priority classes for platform components and reserve resources for system daemons.
tip: QoS class decides eviction order: BestEffort first, then Burstable, Guaranteed last.
a: When a node runs low on memory, the kubelet evicts pods, choosing by quality-of-service class and then by usage relative to requests. A controller pod with no requests or limits is classified best effort and goes first, even though it is critical to the platform. I check the pod's QoS class and the node conditions. To protect it, I set resource requests equal to limits so it is in the guaranteed class, and assign a high priority class so the scheduler and eviction logic favour it over ordinary workloads. At the same time I address the cause of memory pressure: find workloads that run without limits and consume too much, enforce requests and limits through admission policy, and reserve memory for the operating system and kubelet using system-reserved settings. Cluster autoscaling may add nodes if overall capacity is short.
f: What is the QoS eviction order?
What does a priority class do?

q: A cronjob in Kubernetes silently stops running, no recent jobs created. How do you find out why?
sym: CronJob last schedule was days ago. No errors in app logs because no pods are created.
inv: kubectl get cronjob report -o yaml | grep -E 'suspend|lastScheduleTime|schedule|concurrencyPolicy|startingDeadlineSeconds'
cause: A previous job hung and concurrencyPolicy: Forbid prevents new runs; or more than 100 missed schedules triggered the controller to stop scheduling.
fix: # delete the stuck job
kubectl delete job report-28345
# set activeDeadlineSeconds on the job
# set startingDeadlineSeconds
# alert on time since last success
prev: Alert on time since the last successful run, set deadlines and history limits, and avoid Forbid without a timeout.
tip: Monitor for absence. A job that no longer runs generates no errors, only silence.
a: A cronjob that stops producing jobs generates no logs or errors, so the first sign is usually a business process noticing missing output. I look at the cronjob status: is it suspended, when was the last schedule, what is the concurrency policy. A frequent culprit is concurrency policy forbid combined with a previous job that hangs forever, so the controller refuses to start another. Another is missing too many schedules during downtime, where the controller gives up after a number of missed starts unless a starting deadline is configured. I delete the stuck job, which allows new ones to run, and add an active deadline so jobs cannot hang indefinitely. For prevention, I add an alert on the time since the last successful completion, using metrics from kube-state-metrics, set history limits, and add timeouts, so silence becomes a visible signal.
f: Why does silence matter for jobs?
What does startingDeadlineSeconds do?

q: An AWS Lambda function suddenly starts failing with timeouts only for the first request after idle periods. How do you diagnose and improve it?
sym: Occasional very slow first invocation (several seconds), then normal. Users notice sporadic delays.
inv: # look at package size, runtime, VPC config, init code
cause: Cold starts: large package, heavy initialisation (SDK clients, config fetch) and VPC networking add several seconds when a new execution environment starts.
fix: # reduce package, lazy-load, initialise clients outside handler
aws lambda put-provisioned-concurrency-config --function-name fn --qualifier prod --provisioned-concurrent-executions 5
# consider SnapStart for supported runtimes
prev: Track init duration, set provisioned concurrency for latency-sensitive paths, keep functions small and avoid blocking init.
tip: Provisioned concurrency trades cost for predictable latency. Use it only where cold starts hurt users.
a: The pattern of a slow first request after idle time is a cold start: Lambda must create an execution environment, download the code, start the runtime and run initialisation code before handling the request. I confirm with the init duration field in the logs. Contributing factors are a large deployment package, heavy imports, creating many SDK clients or fetching configuration during init, and in some cases VPC attachment. Improvements start with trimming the package and dependencies, lazy-loading rarely used modules, and moving expensive initialisation out of the critical path or caching it. For latency-sensitive endpoints, I configure provisioned concurrency to keep a number of environments warm, accepting the extra cost, or use SnapStart where supported. I monitor the init duration percentiles and cold start rate, and decide per function whether the cost of keeping it warm is justified by the user impact.
f: How do you confirm a cold start?
What is provisioned concurrency?

q: A cloud load balancer health check marks all targets unhealthy right after a security group change, but the app is fine. How do you recover?
sym: All targets unhealthy, 503 from the load balancer. Instances respond locally. Change made 5 minutes ago.
inv: # can LB subnet reach the health check port?
cause: The change removed the inbound rule allowing the load balancer's security group on the health check port.
fix: aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-app --protocol tcp --port 8080 --source-group sg-alb
# verify targets return to healthy
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn $TG
prev: Manage security groups as code with review, reference groups by ID instead of CIDR, and validate connectivity in a post-change check.
tip: CloudTrail tells you exactly which rule changed and who changed it, which speeds up rollback.
a: If the application responds locally but the load balancer reports all targets unhealthy right after a network change, the health check traffic is probably blocked. I check the target health reason, then compare the instance security group rules to what the load balancer needs: the health check port must allow inbound traffic from the load balancer's security group or subnets. CloudTrail shows the recent security group modification, who made it and what was removed. The fix is re-adding the rule, preferably by referencing the load balancer's security group rather than IP ranges, then confirming the targets turn healthy and traffic resumes. I also check network ACLs and route tables in case they were involved. Preventing a repeat means managing security groups in infrastructure as code with peer review and plan output, and adding an automated connectivity test after changes, plus alerts on sudden drops in healthy host count.
f: Why reference security groups by ID?
What does CloudTrail show?

q: Your cloud storage bucket costs spiked because of millions of tiny requests and egress. How do you find the source and stop it?
sym: Storage bill up 5x. Request and data transfer lines dominate. No new features shipped.
inv: # enable and query S3 access logs / CloudTrail data events
athena: select requester, count(*) from s3_logs group by 1 order by 2 desc limit 10
cause: A misconfigured client polls the bucket listing every second, and an unauthenticated public object is being hot-linked by a third party.
fix: # fix the polling client to use events/notifications
# block public access, restrict via CloudFront signed URLs
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket b --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true
prev: Enable cost anomaly detection, put CDN in front of public content, block public access by default and use event notifications instead of polling.
tip: The requester and user agent in access logs usually identify the culprit within minutes.
a: I start with the billing breakdown by usage type to see which component grew: storage, request counts or data transfer out. Then I turn on or query the access logs and data events to see who is making the requests: the requester identity, IP addresses, user agents and the most requested keys. In this case, one internal client lists the bucket continuously, which generates millions of paid list requests, and a popular public file is being hot-linked by a third-party site, creating egress costs. I fix the client to rely on event notifications rather than polling, and I stop the leak by blocking public access, serving public content through a CDN with caching, or requiring signed URLs. To prevent surprises, I set up cost anomaly detection and budget alerts, tag buckets with owners, and review default access settings across accounts.
f: How do you find who makes the requests?
Why use a CDN for public files?

q: A cross-account IAM role assumption suddenly fails with AccessDenied after a policy cleanup. How do you debug it?
sym: sts:AssumeRole denied from account A to role in account B. Worked last week.
cause: The caller's identity policy no longer allows sts:AssumeRole on the target role after a cleanup, while the trust policy requires an ExternalId that was also removed from the caller's configuration.
fix: # restore identity policy permitting sts:AssumeRole on that ARN
# pass ExternalId in the assume-role call
aws sts assume-role --role-arn $ROLE --role-session-name x --external-id abc123
prev: Test IAM cleanups with policy simulation and last-accessed data, and manage roles as code with review.
tip: Cross-account access needs both sides: the caller must be allowed to assume, and the target must trust the caller.
a: A cross-account assume-role requires two permissions to line up: the identity policy of the caller must allow the assume-role action on the target role, and the target role's trust policy must name the caller as a trusted principal, with any conditions satisfied, such as an external ID or multi-factor requirement. Organisation service control policies and permission boundaries can also deny it. I read the CloudTrail event for the denied call, which names the principal and often the reason, and use the policy simulator to check each layer. In this scenario the clean-up removed the allow statement from the caller, and the condition in the trust policy was no longer met. I restore the minimum permission and update the caller to pass the external ID. Afterwards, I improve how IAM changes are made: use last-accessed data before removing permissions, test with simulation, and keep policies in code with review and staged rollout.
f: What two sides must agree?
What can silently deny besides IAM policies?

q: A managed Kubernetes control plane upgrade finished, but nodes are on an old version and some workloads misbehave. How do you manage version skew?
sym: Control plane at 1.30, node groups still at 1.28. Some pods behave oddly, new features unavailable.
inv: kubectl version; kubectl get nodes -o wide
cause: Nodes lag beyond the supported skew (kubelet can be at most a few minor versions behind the API server), so behaviour is undefined.
fix: # upgrade node groups one minor at a time, surge + drain
eksctl upgrade nodegroup --name ng1 --cluster c --kubernetes-version 1.29
# pause risky deploys until aligned
prev: Upgrade control plane and nodes in one planned sequence, automate node rotation, and monitor version drift.
tip: Skew limits exist for a reason. Treat out-of-policy skew as an incident-in-waiting.
a: Kubernetes supports a limited version difference between the control plane and the kubelets, and the older the nodes, the more risk that APIs, features and behaviours mismatch. When I see nodes lagging, I list kubelet versions and compare them to the skew policy. If they are outside it, I treat it as a priority to realign. I upgrade node groups in sequence, one minor version at a time, using surge nodes or new node groups, cordon and drain old nodes while respecting disruption budgets, and verify workloads after each step. Meanwhile I limit risky changes and avoid deploying workloads that depend on new features. To prevent drift, I plan upgrades as a single process covering control plane, nodes and add-ons, automate node replacement on a regular cadence, and alert when node versions fall behind the control plane by more than a set margin.
f: What is version skew?
How do you upgrade nodes safely?

q: Your multi-region failover test worked in staging but the real failover took 40 minutes because of DNS and stale caches. What do you improve?
sym: Primary region failed; traffic took 40 minutes to shift. Some clients still hitting dead region.
inv: # which clients cache DNS beyond TTL (JVM, mobile)
# check failover record config and health check interval
cause: High DNS TTL (1 hour), slow health check thresholds and clients that cache resolution kept routing to the failed region.
fix: # lower TTL to 30-60s on failover records
# health check interval 10s, threshold 2
# use anycast / global load balancer for instant shift
# JVM: -Dnetworkaddress.cache.ttl=30
prev: Run real failover game days with production-like clients, measure end-to-end RTO and fix each contributor.
tip: DNS failover time = detection time + TTL + client caching. Measure all three.
a: Failover time is the sum of detection time, record time-to-live and how long clients cache answers. In the incident the health check needed several slow intervals to declare the region down, the record had a long time-to-live, and some clients, like a Java runtime with default caching, ignored the TTL. I shorten each contributor: quicker health checks with a low failure threshold, a TTL of thirty to sixty seconds on failover records, and client configuration for DNS caching in long-running processes. For faster and more reliable shifting I consider global load balancing or anycast, which moves traffic at the network layer without relying on client DNS behaviour. Importantly, I run realistic failover drills in production or a faithful replica, with real client types, measure the end-to-end recovery time against the target, and repeat until it is met. I also confirm that the secondary region has capacity for the full load.
f: What are the components of failover time?
Why are drills with real clients important?

q: Intermittent connection resets (RST) occur between two services behind a NAT gateway on long-lived idle connections. What is happening?
sym: Connections idle for several minutes then fail with connection reset on first use. Short connections fine.
inv: # NAT gateway idle timeout (e.g. 350s on AWS NAT)
# app connection pool max idle time
cause: The NAT gateway drops idle flows after its timeout; the client still believes the connection is open and sends on a dead flow, which gets an RST.
fix: # enable TCP keepalive shorter than NAT timeout
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time=120
# set pool max idle lifetime < NAT timeout
# add retry on stale connection for idempotent calls
prev: Document infrastructure idle timeouts and configure pools and keepalives below the smallest one in the path.
tip: Every stateful middlebox has an idle timeout. Keepalives and pool lifetimes must be shorter than the shortest.
a: Firewalls, NAT gateways and load balancers keep a state table for each flow and expire entries after an idle timeout. If an application holds a pooled connection idle for longer than that, the middlebox forgets it, and when the client later sends data, the packet either gets a reset or disappears. The symptom is errors on the first request after a quiet period and healthy short-lived connections. I confirm by capturing packets to see the reset and by comparing the idle time with the gateway's documented timeout. The fix is to make the endpoints respect the shortest timeout in the path: enable TCP keepalives at an interval below it, or set the connection pool's maximum idle time lower, and add a safe retry on a stale connection for idempotent requests. Prevention is documenting each hop's timeout and standardising client libraries' pool settings.
f: Why does the first request after idle fail?
What should keepalive be relative to the NAT timeout?

q: Packets are being dropped between two VPCs connected by peering, but only for large payloads. How do you diagnose MTU and fragmentation problems?
sym: Small requests succeed, large responses hang. ICMP ping works. Path crosses a VPN or tunnel.
inv: ping -M do -s 1472 target   # find max unfragmented size
ip link show eth0 | grep mtu
cause: A tunnel with a smaller MTU drops oversized packets with DF set, and ICMP fragmentation-needed messages are blocked by a security rule, so path MTU discovery fails.
fix: # allow ICMP type 3 code 4
# clamp TCP MSS on the tunnel
iptables -t mangle -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu
# or lower interface MTU
prev: Document MTU along each path, never block ICMP fragmentation-needed, and test large transfers after network changes.
tip: The classic sign is: connect works, small data works, large data hangs. Think MTU.
a: If handshakes and small messages succeed but larger transfers stall, I suspect a path MTU problem. Some link along the path, such as a VPN tunnel or overlay network, has a smaller maximum packet size than the endpoints assume. Normally a router that cannot forward an oversized packet with the do-not-fragment flag set sends back an ICMP fragmentation-needed message, and the sender reduces its packet size. If a firewall or security rule drops that ICMP message, the sender never learns and keeps retransmitting big packets that vanish. I confirm by pinging with the do-not-fragment flag at various sizes to find the largest that passes, and capturing traffic for the ICMP messages. The fix is to permit the required ICMP type, and clamp the TCP maximum segment size on the tunnel so the endpoints negotiate smaller segments, or set a consistent MTU. I then test with large transfers.
f: What is path MTU discovery?
Why do small packets work?

q: Users in one country can't reach your service while others can. How do you determine if it is routing, DNS, CDN or blocking?
sym: Reports from users in one region/ISP: timeouts or wrong certificates. Others fine.
inv: mtr -rw app.example.com   # from affected region probe
# check CDN edge logs for that POP
cause: A regional ISP resolver returns an outdated IP for the domain, pointing to a decommissioned address range.
fix: # lower TTL and wait/notify ISP, publish via alternative resolvers
# keep old IP responding with redirect during migration
# status page + support guidance (public DNS)
prev: Keep old addresses alive through migrations for at least the max TTL, monitor from multiple geographies and test through major resolvers.
tip: Compare answers from public resolvers and the ISP's resolver. Different answers point straight at DNS.
a: A regional problem has a limited set of causes, so I test from the affected region using external probes or a volunteer. I compare DNS answers from public resolvers and the local ISP resolver, check whether the TCP connection and TLS handshake succeed to the right address, trace the network path to see where packets stop, and look at CDN logs to see if the requests arrive at the edge. If the ISP resolver returns an outdated address, traffic goes to the wrong place; if the TLS certificate is wrong, something is intercepting; if the path ends at a particular network, it is a routing issue. In this case it is stale DNS. Mitigation includes keeping the old address serving or redirecting during transitions, lowering TTLs ahead of changes, advising users to use alternative resolvers, and contacting the ISP. Monitoring from several geographies catches regional breakage early.
f: How do you test from a specific region?
How do you avoid stale DNS during migrations?

q: A newly added microservice cannot reach the database although security groups look right. How do you find the block?
sym: Connection timeout from new service to DB on port 5432. Existing services connect fine.
inv: # check route tables and subnets for the new service
cause: The new service sits in a subnet whose network ACL does not allow ephemeral return ports, or lacks a route to the database subnet.
fix: # add NACL rules for return traffic (1024-65535) and DB port
# or place service in the correct subnet group
aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry ...
prev: Define network layout in code with reusable modules and run reachability analysis in CI for new services.
tip: Security groups are stateful, but network ACLs are stateless. They need explicit rules in both directions.
a: When security groups look correct, I check the other layers on the path. First, routing: does the new subnet's route table have a route to the database's subnet, or does the service run in a different network with no peering? Next, network ACLs, which are stateless, so they need explicit rules for the request and the response ephemeral port ranges; a missing return rule makes connections hang. Then I consider the database's own firewall settings, DNS resolution to a private address, and any endpoint policies. Reachability analysis tools can trace the path and point to the blocking component without guessing. Once the missing rule or route is added, I verify with a connection test and application logs. To avoid repeating this, I define networking with reusable modules, so new services inherit tested subnet, route and rule configurations, and I include automated reachability checks in the pipeline.
f: How do NACLs differ from security groups?
What is reachability analysis?

q: TLS handshakes to an internal service start failing across the fleet at midnight. Certificates look valid. What else could it be?
sym: x509 errors at 00:00 UTC across many clients. Server cert valid for 90 more days.
inv: # check the intermediate and root in the chain
cause: The intermediate CA certificate expired at midnight, though the leaf certificate was valid; servers did not send the new intermediate.
fix: # install the renewed intermediate in the chain served
# update trust bundles in clients if root changed
# restart services to load the chain
prev: Monitor expiry for every certificate in the chain, including intermediates and roots, and test chain validation from clients.
tip: A valid leaf does not help if any certificate above it in the chain has expired.
a: Many teams monitor the expiry of the server certificate and forget everything above it. The client validates the entire chain, so an expired intermediate or root certificate breaks all connections that use it, typically at a precise time like midnight. I view the chain served by the endpoint and check the validity dates of each certificate, verify against the trust bundle, and also confirm clocks are synchronised, since skewed time causes similar errors. The remedy is installing the renewed intermediate in the chain the servers present, updating client trust stores if the root changed, and reloading or restarting services. For prevention, I monitor expiry dates for every certificate in the chain and in trust bundles, test validation using realistic clients, automate issuance and chain deployment, and keep a calendar for CA events and rotation procedures.
f: Why check intermediates?
How can clock skew look like cert failure?

q: A server has plenty of free disk blocks but cannot create files because it has run out of inodes. How do you find and fix it?
sym: 'No space left on device' while df -h shows 30% used. Application cannot write new files.
inv: for d in /var/*; do echo $d $(find $d -xdev | wc -l); done | sort -k2 -n | tail
cause: Millions of tiny session or cache files accumulated in one directory without cleanup, exhausting the inode table.
fix: # delete in batches to avoid blocking
find /var/lib/php/sessions -type f -mtime +1 -delete
# configure cleanup (tmpreaper/logrotate/app GC)
# longer term: recreate FS with more inodes or use object storage
prev: Monitor inode usage as well as blocks, add retention to caches and sessions, and choose appropriate filesystem parameters.
tip: Deleting millions of files with rm * may fail with argument list too long. Use find -delete.
a: The error message is the same as a full disk, but the cause differs: every file needs an inode, and the filesystem has a fixed number of them. Checking inode usage with the inode flag on df confirms it. To find the offender, I count files per directory, looking for places that generate many tiny files such as session stores, cache directories, mail spools or temporary files from a runaway job. I delete the old files in batches using find with a delete action and an age filter, taking care not to remove active ones, and fix the root cause by adding a retention policy or cleanup job. If the workload legitimately needs enormous numbers of small files, I consider creating the filesystem with more inodes or switching to object storage or a database. I also add inode usage to monitoring and alerts.
f: How does df -i help?
Why use find -delete instead of rm *?

q: A process is stuck in uninterruptible sleep (D state) and cannot be killed. What causes this and how do you recover?
sym: ps shows D state processes, load average climbing, kill -9 has no effect.
cause: Processes wait on IO that never completes because a network filesystem server is unreachable or a disk is failing.
fix: # restore the storage path (network, server, multipath)
# or lazy unmount as last resort
umount -l /mnt/data
# if hardware: fail over and replace the disk
# reboot only when nothing else works
prev: Use soft/timeout mount options where safe, monitor storage latency and avoid putting critical paths on fragile network mounts.
tip: D-state processes count toward load average even with idle CPU, which explains high load with a quiet CPU.
a: The D state means the process is blocked in the kernel waiting for IO and cannot be interrupted, so signals, even kill nine, are not handled until the operation returns. It typically signals trouble below the application: an unreachable NFS server, a hung storage array or failing disk, or a driver problem. These blocked processes still count toward the load average, which is why load can be high while the CPU is idle. I look at the wait channel and kernel stack to see what they are waiting on, check mounts and storage latency, and the kernel log for errors. Recovery means fixing the underlying path, for example restoring network connectivity to the file server or failing over the storage. If that is impossible, a lazy unmount can detach the mount point, and as a last resort a reboot. Prevention includes careful mount options, monitoring and avoiding single points of failure.
f: Why does load rise with idle CPU?
What is a lazy unmount?

q: A time-sensitive application fails authentication because server clocks drifted by minutes. How do you fix time sync and prevent it?
sym: Kerberos / JWT / TOTP failures, log timestamps out of order across hosts, certificate 'not yet valid' errors.
cause: NTP daemon stopped after a config change and VMs drifted; firewall blocked UDP 123 to time servers.
fix: systemctl enable --now chronyd
chronyc makestep
# allow UDP 123 to internal NTP servers
# verify offset < 100 ms
prev: Run internal NTP sources, monitor clock offset on every host, and alert when drift exceeds a small threshold.
tip: Prefer stepping slowly (slew) for running services; use makestep carefully since time jumps can break applications.
a: Clock drift causes confusing failures: tokens appear expired or not yet valid, Kerberos rejects tickets, certificates look invalid and distributed logs cannot be correlated. I check the synchronisation state on affected hosts, comparing time against a trusted source, and look at the time service's sources and offset. The usual causes are a stopped or misconfigured daemon, firewall rules blocking the protocol port, or virtual machines paused and resumed. I restore the service, ensure it can reach reliable servers, and correct the offset. Large jumps can disturb running applications, so I prefer gradual adjustment for small drift and a controlled step for large ones, possibly restarting sensitive services. For prevention I deploy redundant internal time servers, configure all hosts consistently through configuration management, export the clock offset as a metric, and alert when it exceeds a small threshold such as a hundred milliseconds.
f: Why are token failures a time symptom?
Step vs slew?

q: After a kernel update and reboot, a server's network interface names changed and services bound to the old interface fail. What happened?
sym: eth0 became ens5; static config and firewall rules reference the old name; no network after reboot.
inv: # console access needed if SSH is down
cause: Predictable interface naming or a changed driver/PCI order renamed the NIC; configs matched by name.
fix: # match by MAC address in netplan
match: macaddress: 0a:1b:2c:3d:4e:5f   set-name: eth0
netplan apply
# update firewall rules to the new name
prev: Match interfaces by MAC or use persistent names, test reboots after kernel updates and keep out-of-band console access.
tip: Always have console or out-of-band access before rebooting a remote server after kernel or network changes.
a: Modern systemd systems name network interfaces based on hardware topology, and a kernel, driver or virtual hardware change can alter that name, so the configuration that referred to the old name no longer matches and the interface stays unconfigured. With SSH down, I use the cloud console or out-of-band management to log in, list the interfaces and see what they are called now, and look at the boot log for rename messages. The quick fix is to adjust the configuration to the new name or, better, match the device by its MAC address and assign a stable name, then reapply the network configuration and update firewall and application bindings that referenced the name. To prevent the problem, I use persistent naming rules or MAC-based matching, test reboots after kernel upgrades in a staging environment, roll out updates gradually, and keep console access available.
f: Why can interface names change?
How do you configure by MAC?

q: A Java service is repeatedly killed by the OOM killer although its heap is capped well below the container memory limit. Why?
sym: Container OOMKilled, Xmx=2g, limit=3g. Heap graphs look fine.
cause: Non-heap memory (metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, code cache, native libraries) plus a high thread count pushes total RSS over the limit.
fix: # size heap to ~60-70% of the limit
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65
# cap direct memory and metaspace
-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=256m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m
# reduce thread count / stack size
prev: Enable native memory tracking in testing, size containers using measured RSS under load and alert on container memory working set.
tip: The heap is only part of the JVM's memory. Budget for metaspace, threads, buffers and the runtime itself.
a: The container limit applies to total resident memory of the process, not the Java heap. The maximum heap setting caps only one region; the JVM also uses metaspace for class metadata, a stack for every thread, direct buffers for network and file IO, the JIT code cache, garbage collector structures and native libraries. With a large number of threads or heavy direct buffer use, the total can exceed the limit even when the heap looks healthy, and the kernel kills the container. I diagnose using native memory tracking and the cgroup memory statistics. The fix is leaving headroom: set the heap as a percentage of the container memory, around sixty to seventy percent, cap direct memory and metaspace, and control thread counts. I size containers based on measured resident memory under realistic load and monitor the working set, not just the heap, with alerts before reaching the limit.
f: What is outside the heap?
How do you size container memory for a JVM?

q: A pipeline suddenly fails to pull base images with 'toomanyrequests' rate-limit errors. How do you fix it right now and permanently?
sym: docker pull fails: 'You have reached your pull rate limit'. Builds blocked across teams.
inv: # which jobs pull most? shared runner IP?
cause: Many CI jobs behind a shared NAT IP make anonymous pulls and exhaust the public registry quota.
fix: # authenticate pulls with a paid account / token
docker login -u ci -p $TOKEN
# configure a pull-through cache / mirror
# use internal registry for base images
prev: Mirror public images into an internal registry, pin by digest and reduce pulls with layer caching.
tip: A pull-through cache also protects you from registry outages and deleted upstream tags.
a: Public registries limit anonymous pulls per IP address, and CI runners often share a few outbound addresses, so a busy day can consume the allowance and block every build. The immediate fix is authenticating pulls, which gives a much higher quota per account, by adding a credential to the runners and the Docker daemon. The permanent solution is to stop depending on the public registry at build time: set up a pull-through cache or mirror inside our network, or copy the base images we use into our own registry, scanning and signing them at the same time. Builds then reference the internal registry, pin images by digest for reproducibility, and benefit from caching, speed and independence from outages or removed tags. I also reduce unnecessary pulls with layer caching on runners and monitor for registry errors in CI metrics so I see the problem before developers complain.
f: Why do shared runners hit limits?
What does a pull-through cache give?

q: A deployment succeeds but the application serves the old version for some users for hours. How do you find the cause?
sym: Pipeline green, new version live in some regions, others still show old behaviour.
inv: curl -s https://app/version; for r in eu us ap; do curl -s https://$r.app/version; done
kubectl get deploy -A -o wide | grep app
# check image tags: latest vs digest
cause: The deployment used the mutable latest tag and a node cached the old image with imagePullPolicy IfNotPresent; the CDN also cached the old bundle for 24 hours.
fix: # deploy by immutable tag/digest
image: registry/app@sha256:abc...
# purge CDN and use content-hashed filenames
aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id D --paths '/*'
prev: Never deploy mutable tags, use hashed asset names, and add a post-deploy check that verifies the running version in every region.
tip: Expose the build version in a header or endpoint so you can verify what is actually serving traffic.
a: A green pipeline only says the deploy command succeeded, not that every user receives the new version. I first check which version each region, pod and CDN edge actually serves, using a version endpoint or response header. Two classic causes appear: mutable image tags such as latest combined with a pull policy that reuses a cached image on a node, so some pods run old code; and caching of static assets or API responses at a CDN or browser with long lifetimes, so users keep getting old bundles. The fixes are deploying immutable references by digest or unique tag, using content-hashed filenames for assets so a new build means a new URL, setting sensible cache headers, and invalidating the CDN when needed. I add a post-deployment verification step that queries the version in every region and fails the pipeline if they disagree.
f: Why avoid the latest tag?
How do hashed filenames help?

q: A monorepo CI run takes two hours because it builds and tests everything on every commit. How do you cut it down safely?
sym: Developers wait hours for feedback, merge queue backed up, teams skip tests locally.
inv: # profile pipeline stages and critical path
# which tests fail rarely / are slowest
# what changed vs what is built
cause: No change-based selection, no remote cache, serial test execution and heavy end-to-end tests run on every commit.
fix: # affected-only builds with dependency graph
nx affected --target=test
# remote build cache
# shard tests across runners in parallel
# move slow e2e to merge queue / nightly
prev: Track pipeline duration as an SLO, review the slowest jobs monthly and keep a fast pre-merge tier plus a thorough post-merge tier.
tip: Fast feedback beats exhaustive feedback on every commit. Run the thorough suite where it counts, but still run it.
a: First I measure: break the pipeline into stages to find the critical path and the slowest jobs. Then I apply layered improvements. Change-based selection uses the dependency graph to build and test only the projects affected by a commit, with full runs on the main branch or for shared changes. A remote cache stores build and test results keyed by inputs, so unchanged work is reused. Tests are sharded and run in parallel across multiple runners, and slow end-to-end suites move from every commit to a merge queue or nightly run, while a fast smoke and unit tier gives quick pre-merge feedback. I also fix flaky tests since retries add time. To avoid trading quality for speed, the complete suite still runs before release and on the main branch, and I track pipeline duration and failure escape rate as metrics, so I notice if the optimisation lets bugs through.
f: What is affected-only testing?
What stays in the pre-merge tier?

q: A Terraform pipeline applied a change in the wrong order, destroying a load balancer before its replacement existed. How do you recover and design around it?
sym: Brief production outage: LB deleted, new LB created after; DNS now points at nothing for several minutes.
inv: # review the plan output that was approved
cause: A change forced replacement of the load balancer, and the default order is destroy then create; the plan was approved without noticing the replacement.
fix: # apply with create_before_destroy where possible
lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }
# use unique name_prefix to avoid conflicts
# manually switch DNS to new LB, verify
prev: Review plans for replacement markers, add policy checks that block replacement of critical resources, and use blue/green for load balancers.
tip: Search the plan for 'replace' and 'destroy'. Make approvers look at those lines first.
a: Terraform's default behaviour when an attribute forces replacement is to destroy the old resource and then create the new one, which for something in the traffic path means downtime. The change was approved without anyone noticing the replacement marker in a long plan. To recover, I verify the new load balancer is healthy, update DNS or listeners as needed, and confirm that traffic is restored. To prevent a repeat, I use the lifecycle setting to create the replacement before destroying the old one, with names that avoid conflicts, or design blue-green load balancers so a switch is a controlled traffic move. Process fixes matter too: plan summaries that highlight destroys and replacements, policy-as-code that blocks or requires extra approval for replacing critical resources, and protecting production resources with prevent-destroy and deletion protection. Approvers are trained to read the replacement lines first.
f: What does create_before_destroy do?
How do you make plans reviewable?

q: A dependency update bot merged a minor version bump that broke production because the library changed behaviour. How do you make automation safer?
sym: Auto-merged dependency PR passed unit tests but changed rounding in a pricing library; wrong prices shown.
inv: # what tests would have caught it?
# check which services consume the lib
cause: A semantic change in a minor release was not covered by tests, and auto-merge had no canary or staged rollout.
fix: # pin and revert to the previous version
git revert <bot-merge>
# add characterisation tests for pricing
# staged rollout of dependency updates
prev: Auto-merge only patch updates with strong test coverage, require canary deployments, and add contract tests for critical calculations.
tip: Semver is a promise, not a guarantee. Critical paths need tests that pin their expected behaviour.
a: Dependency automation is valuable for security and maintenance, but it moves risk into the pipeline. After reverting and restoring correct behaviour, I analyse why the tests did not catch the change. The pricing logic depended on library behaviour that no test pinned down, so a subtle rounding difference passed. I add characterisation tests with representative inputs and expected outputs for critical calculations. I also tighten the automation policy: auto-merge only low-risk updates, such as patch versions with high coverage, require human review for minor or major updates in critical libraries, group updates in smaller batches, and deploy through a canary stage with business metric monitoring so anomalies are caught on a small share of traffic. Reading release notes for libraries on critical paths and keeping lockfiles committed ensure the exact versions in production are known and reproducible.
f: Why is semver not a guarantee?
What should be auto-merged?

q: Replication lag on a read replica grows steadily during a nightly batch job, causing stale reads. How do you handle it?
sym: Replica lag climbs to 20 minutes between 01:00 and 03:00; users see missing recent updates.
inv: select pid, now()-xact_start from pg_stat_activity where state<>'idle' order by 2 desc;
cause: The batch job produces a huge volume of WAL, and long analytical queries on the replica conflict with replay.
fix: # batch in smaller transactions with sleeps
# route analytics to a dedicated replica
# tune max_standby_streaming_delay and hot_standby_feedback
# read-your-writes: send critical reads to primary
prev: Alert on replication lag, separate workloads by replica, and design read paths to tolerate or avoid stale data.
tip: Replicas are eventually consistent. Decide which reads need the primary.
a: Replication lag happens when the replica cannot apply changes as fast as the primary generates them, or when queries on the replica conflict with the replay of changes. A nightly batch job writes a large volume of data, and heavy queries on the replica may also hold back replay. I check the lag metric over time, the write volume on the primary, and long-running queries on the replica. Mitigations include splitting the batch into smaller transactions with pauses to smooth the write rate, dedicating a separate replica for long analytical queries, tuning the replay conflict settings with an understanding of the trade-offs, and giving the replica enough IO. On the application side, I route reads that require the latest data, such as immediately after a write, to the primary, and use lag-aware routing that avoids replicas that are too far behind. Alerts on lag provide early warning.
f: Why do queries conflict with replay?
Which reads need the primary?

q: A Kafka consumer group is stuck rebalancing constantly and throughput collapses. What do you check?
sym: Frequent rebalances, consumer lag grows, logs show 'Revoking previously assigned partitions' repeatedly.
cause: Message processing takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, so the broker thinks the consumer is dead and triggers a rebalance, which repeats.
fix: # reduce max.poll.records or speed up processing
max.poll.interval.ms=600000  max.poll.records=100
# use cooperative sticky assignor
# stop autoscaling flapping consumers
# static membership group.instance.id
prev: Alert on rebalance frequency and lag, decouple slow processing with worker pools, and use static membership for stable deployments.
tip: Each rebalance pauses consumption for the group. Frequent rebalances turn into a throughput outage.
a: In Kafka, consumers must call poll regularly. If processing a batch takes longer than the maximum poll interval, the group coordinator assumes the consumer has failed, removes it and triggers a rebalance, during which all consumers in the group pause. The consumer comes back, joins, and the cycle repeats, so throughput collapses and lag grows. I check the consumer logs for poll timeout messages, compare batch processing time with the configured interval, and look for external triggers like pods restarting or autoscaling flapping. I fix it by reducing the number of records per poll, speeding up or parallelising processing outside the polling thread, or increasing the interval within reason. Cooperative rebalancing and static membership reduce disruption from deployments and restarts. I add alerts on rebalance rate and lag, and load test with realistic message sizes and downstream latency.
f: Why does a rebalance pause the group?
What is static membership?

q: Elasticsearch cluster turns yellow then red after a node restart, and search results are incomplete. How do you recover?
sym: Cluster health red; unassigned shards; some indices unavailable.
cause: Disk watermark exceeded on remaining nodes so shards cannot be allocated, and replica count was zero for one index so its data was only on the restarted node.
fix: # free disk or add node; clear watermark block
curl -XPUT localhost:9200/_cluster/settings -d '{"transient":{"cluster.routing.allocation.disk.watermark.low":"90%"}}'
# retry allocation
curl -XPOST 'localhost:9200/_cluster/reroute?retry_failed=true'
# restore missing index from snapshot if needed
prev: Keep at least one replica for important indices, maintain disk headroom, take snapshots and use allocation awareness.
tip: The allocation explain API tells you exactly why a shard is not assigned. Start there.
a: Red means at least one primary shard is unassigned, so some data is unavailable. I begin with the cluster health and list the unassigned shards, then use the allocation explanation to see why: not enough disk space under the watermark settings, no node with the right attributes, a node still missing, or corrupted data. In this case the remaining nodes crossed their disk watermark, so Elasticsearch refused to allocate shards to them, and an index with no replicas lost its only copy when the node went down. I free up disk or add capacity, adjust the watermarks temporarily if safe, and trigger a reroute to retry allocation. If a primary's data is truly lost, I restore that index from a snapshot. Afterwards I ensure important indices have replicas, monitor disk usage with margins, take regular snapshots and test restores, and use shard allocation awareness across zones.
f: What do watermarks do?
Why have replicas?

q: A Redis instance used as a cache starts evicting keys and the database load triples. What is going on and how do you respond?
sym: Hit ratio drops, evicted_keys increases, DB CPU spikes, latency rises.
cause: A new feature stores large objects without TTL, filling memory to maxmemory so the allkeys-lru policy evicts hot keys.
fix: # add TTLs, cap object sizes
# increase memory or shard
redis-cli config set maxmemory 8gb
# protect DB with request coalescing and rate limiting
# remove the large keys
prev: Alert on hit ratio and evictions, set TTLs by default, review key patterns, and protect the database with stampede controls.
tip: A cache is a performance layer and often a hidden capacity dependency. Know what happens to the DB when hit ratio drops.
a: When Redis reaches its memory limit, the eviction policy removes keys, and if the evicted entries are the hot ones, the cache hit ratio drops and requests fall through to the database, which can overload it. I check memory usage, the eviction counters and hit ratio trends, find large keys that consume the space, and see what changed recently. Here a new feature stores sizeable objects with no expiry. Immediate actions are increasing the memory limit or adding shards if possible, removing or shrinking the offending keys, and protecting the database with rate limiting, request coalescing so identical misses result in one query, and temporary load shedding. The permanent fix includes setting a default TTL, bounding object size, choosing an eviction policy that matches usage, and monitoring hit ratio, evictions and memory with alerts. I also load test the system with a cold cache to know its true capacity.
f: Why does eviction overload the DB?
What is request coalescing?

q: A data pipeline silently produced duplicate records after a retry, and downstream reports are inflated. How do you detect, fix and prevent it?
sym: Revenue report 12% too high. Row counts in the warehouse exceed source counts.
inv: select id, count(*) from fact_orders group by id having count(*) > 1;
# compare source vs destination counts per day
# check job logs for retries / at-least-once delivery
select batch_id, count(*) from load_audit group by 1;
cause: The loader uses at-least-once delivery and inserts without a unique key, so a retried batch loaded twice.
fix: # dedupe with window function and rebuild affected partitions
delete from fact_orders where ctid not in (select min(ctid) from fact_orders group by id);
# make loads idempotent: MERGE/upsert on natural key
# add unique constraint / dedup in ETL
prev: Design pipelines to be idempotent, add reconciliation checks between source and sink and alert on count mismatch.
tip: At-least-once plus idempotent writes gives effectively-once results. Retries without idempotency create duplicates.
a: To detect the problem, I compare record counts and checksums between source and destination per partition or day, and query for duplicate keys. The logs show that a batch load failed halfway and was retried. Because delivery is at least once and the insert has no uniqueness guarantee, rows loaded twice. To fix existing data, I identify the affected partitions, deduplicate using the business key, or reload those partitions from the source in an idempotent way, and re-run downstream reports, informing consumers about the corrected numbers. To prevent recurrence, I make loads idempotent using merge or upsert on a natural key or batch identifier, track processed batch IDs in an audit table, add uniqueness constraints where the store supports them, and run automated reconciliation checks after each load that alert on mismatches. Data quality tests become part of the pipeline.
f: What makes a load idempotent?
How do you reconcile source and sink?

q: Your alerts fire correctly but the on-call can't tell which customer-facing feature is affected. How do you make alerts more informative?
sym: Alert text: 'High error rate on service X'. Responder spends 15 minutes finding impact and owner.
inv: kubectl get prometheusrule -o yaml | grep -A10 annotations
# do alerts link dashboards, runbooks, owners?
# can we map service to user journey?
cause: Alerts have no context: no impact description, severity rationale, dashboard or runbook link, and no mapping to the user journey.
fix: annotations: summary: 'Checkout errors > 2% (card payments failing)'
dashboard: https://grafana/d/checkout
runbook: https://wiki/runbooks/checkout-errors
labels: team: payments, severity: page
# include top error and recent deploy
prev: Alert templates with required fields, and a review of alerts after every incident for missing context.
tip: A good alert answers: what is broken for whom, how bad, where to look, and what to do first.
a: An alert that only says a service has a high error rate forces the responder to rediscover context under pressure. I improve alerts by making them answer four questions: what is broken from the user's point of view, how severe it is, where to look, and what to do first.
