Practically, each alert carries a human summary with the user impact, labels for the owning team and severity, links to the relevant dashboard and runbook, and where possible dynamic context like the top error message and the most recent deployment. I map services to user journeys, so alerts speak in terms such as card payments failing rather than internal names. Templates enforce required fields, and after every incident I review whether the alert helped or delayed diagnosis, then update it. Alert quality becomes a tracked item in on-call retrospectives.
f: What should every alert include?
How do you map services to journeys?

q: Logs from one service stopped appearing in your central logging system an hour ago. How do you find where the pipeline is broken?
sym: Kibana/Loki shows no logs from service payments since 10:14. Service is running and healthy.
inv: kubectl get pods -n logging; kubectl logs ds/fluent-bit -n logging | tail
# did log format or volume change?
cause: The service began emitting very large JSON lines after a deploy; the agent dropped them as oversized and the backend rate-limited the stream.
fix: # cap line size in the app, fix the log message
# raise agent buffer / max line size cautiously
# re-ship from node files if still available
# add the stream to rate limit allowlist if justified
prev: Monitor log pipeline health (ingest rate per service, drops, lag), alert on silent services, and set size limits at the source.
tip: Alert on the absence of logs from services that should always log. Silence is a signal.
a: I trace the path from source to storage. First I confirm the application still writes logs locally, using the container logs, so I know whether the problem is before or after collection. Then I check the collection agent on the node for errors, buffering and dropped records, and finally the backend's ingestion metrics for rejected or rate-limited streams. Here the deployment changed the log format and started emitting oversized lines that the agent or backend rejected. I fix the source by limiting message size and correcting the verbose log statement, adjust limits cautiously if the large lines are legitimate, and recover missing logs from node files if they are still available. To avoid a blind spot next time, I monitor the pipeline itself: ingest rate per service, drop counters and agent lag, and alert when a service that normally logs goes quiet.
f: How do you locate the break in the pipeline?
Why alert on missing logs?

q: Your trace sampling is set to 1% and the intermittent error you are chasing never shows up. How do you capture the interesting traces?
sym: Rare failures (0.05%) are invisible in traces; logs lack context to link requests.
inv: # are errors and slow traces force-kept?
# error rate vs traces with error status
cause: Head-based random sampling decides before the outcome is known, so rare errors are almost never kept.
fix: # tail-based sampling in the collector

processors: tail_sampling: policies: [{name: errors, type: status_code, status_code: {status_codes: [ERROR]}}, {name: slow, type: latency, latency: {threshold_ms: 1000}}, {name: base, type: probabilistic, probabilistic: {sampling_percentage: 1}}]
prev: Use tail-based sampling to keep all errors and slow requests, add exemplars linking metrics to traces and keep trace IDs in logs.
tip: Sample after you know the outcome. Keep every error and every slow trace, and a small random baseline.
a: Head-based sampling decides at the start of a request whether to record it, before knowing whether it will fail or be slow, so rare problems are kept only at the sampling rate. For a failure occurring in half a percent of requests and a one percent sample, I would see almost none. The better approach is tail-based sampling: collectors buffer spans for a request, and once the trace is complete, apply policies, keeping all traces with errors, all traces slower than a threshold, and a small random fraction for baseline comparison. That keeps costs under control while preserving the interesting data. It needs enough collector memory and routing so all spans of a trace reach the same collector. I also add exemplars so metric spikes link directly to example traces, and include the trace ID in log lines, so any log can be pivoted to its trace.
f: Why does head sampling miss rare errors?
What does tail sampling need?

q: After enabling debug logging to chase a bug, the application becomes slower and the log bill jumps. How should you debug in production safely?
sym: Latency up 20% and logging costs triple after switching the log level to debug fleet-wide.
inv: # measure overhead: latency and CPU vs log volume
kubectl top pods; check log lines per second
# is debug enabled everywhere or only needed paths?
cause: Debug logging was enabled globally, producing high volume synchronously on hot paths.
fix: # revert to info; enable debug for one pod or one user via dynamic log level
curl -X POST app/admin/loglevel -d 'logger=payments&level=debug&ttl=15m'
# use sampling and async appenders
# use traces / feature-flagged diagnostics instead
prev: Support dynamic, scoped, time-limited log levels, structured logs, and rely on traces and metrics before verbose logging.
tip: Make debug logging expire automatically so it is never left on by accident.
a: Turning on debug level for everything is a blunt instrument: log volume explodes, hot code paths slow down because of formatting and IO, and ingestion costs rise. I revert to a normal level and use a more targeted approach. The application should support changing log levels at runtime for specific loggers and for a limited scope, such as one instance, one tenant or requests with a particular header, with an automatic expiry like fifteen minutes. Asynchronous appenders and sampling reduce overhead. Often traces, metrics and profiling answer the question without verbose logs, and a feature-flagged diagnostic mode can capture exactly the data needed. Everything gets recorded in the incident or investigation notes. Afterwards I ensure that logs are structured and include the identifiers needed to investigate without debug mode in the future.
f: Why should debug logging expire?
What alternatives exist to verbose logs?

q: A queue consumer fleet autoscaled to 200 pods but throughput didn't improve, and the database is struggling. What went wrong?
sym: Lag stays high despite 10x consumers; DB CPU at 100%, lock waits and connection errors.
inv: select wait_event_type, count(*) from pg_stat_activity group by 1;
cause: The bottleneck is the database, not the consumers. More consumers add contention and connection pressure, reducing total throughput.
fix: # cap max replicas to what the DB can sustain
# batch writes, add indexes, use a connection pooler
# scale the DB or partition the workload
# apply backpressure: pause consumption when DB latency high
prev: Load test the whole path to find the true bottleneck, set autoscaler maximums from downstream capacity, and implement backpressure.
tip: Scaling a stage that isn't the bottleneck makes the real bottleneck worse.
a: Autoscaling the consumers assumed that consumer capacity was the limit. In reality the shared database is the bottleneck, so adding consumers only added more concurrent queries, lock contention and connections, which slowed everything, a classic case of congestion collapse. I confirm by looking at database CPU, waits and connection counts alongside per-message processing time, and by seeing that throughput stops rising or falls as concurrency increases. The fix is to cap the consumer count at what the database can sustain, then improve the actual bottleneck: batching writes, adding indexes, using a pooler, optimising queries, and scaling the database vertically or partitioning data. I add backpressure so consumers slow or pause when database latency rises, and set autoscaler limits based on downstream capacity. A full-path load test would have shown the real constraint before it hit production.
f: How do you find the true bottleneck?
What is backpressure?

q: Your service handles peak traffic fine in load tests but fails in production at half that load. What differences do you look for?
sym: Production degrades at 50% of tested peak. Staging passes with margin.
inv: # compare environments: data size, caches, topology, config
# request mix in prod vs test
# third-party calls mocked in test, real in prod
# noisy neighbours, shared limits, DNS, connection limits
cause: The load test used a uniform request mix on a small dataset with mocked dependencies; production has a skewed mix, large data, real downstream rate limits and cold caches.
fix: # replay production traffic shape (shadow/replay)
# test with production-size data
# include real or realistic dependency latencies and limits
# fix the discovered limit (e.g. downstream rate limit)
prev: Treat load test realism as a requirement: data volume, traffic mix, dependencies, cache state and concurrency.
tip: A load test is only as good as its model of production. Validate the model against real traffic.
a: A passing load test proves the system handles the test, not production. Typical differences are the request mix, because real users hit expensive endpoints and large tenants more than a uniform script does; data volume, since a small test database fits in memory and uses fast indexes; dependencies mocked in the test but real in production with latency and rate limits; cache state, such as warm caches in the test and cold or churning ones in production; and infrastructure differences like fewer replicas, shared noisy neighbours, connection limits and DNS behaviour. I compare telemetry from the failing production period against the test run to find which resource saturates first. Then I improve the test by replaying captured production traffic, using production-sized data, and including realistic downstream behaviour. After fixing the limiting factor, I rerun the test and validate its predictions against actual production load.
f: Why does data size matter in tests?
How do you make load tests realistic?

q: A latency-sensitive service shares nodes with batch jobs, and every batch run causes latency spikes. How do you isolate them?
sym: p99 spikes coincide with batch jobs starting on the same node pool; CPU shares and cache contention.
inv: kubectl get pods -o wide --all-namespaces | grep node-7
# CPU throttling for the latency service
cause: Batch pods are Burstable with low requests, consuming bursty CPU, memory bandwidth and disk IO, while the latency service lacks guaranteed resources.
fix: # dedicated node pool with taints for batch
tolerations + nodeSelector for batch jobs
# Guaranteed QoS and CPU pinning for latency-critical pods
# priority classes; set batch requests realistically
# IO limits for batch
prev: Separate workload classes by node pool, set priorities and realistic requests and monitor throttling and noisy neighbour signals.
tip: Shared nodes share caches, memory bandwidth and disk IO, which requests and limits do not fully isolate.
a: Mixing latency-sensitive and batch workloads on the same machine invites interference. CPU limits and requests share the processor time, but not all resources are isolated: cache, memory bandwidth, disk and network IO are shared, and bursts from a batch job cause jitter in the service. I confirm by correlating spikes with the batch schedule and examining throttling metrics for the service. The most reliable fix is physical separation: a dedicated node pool for batch workloads with taints and tolerations, so they never land on the nodes used by the latency-critical service. For the service itself I use requests equal to limits for guaranteed quality of service, and consider CPU pinning. Priority classes ensure that the service wins under contention, and I set realistic requests on batch jobs and IO limits. Continued monitoring of tail latency and throttling verifies the result.
f: What resources aren't isolated by limits?
Why use a dedicated node pool?

q: You must reduce infrastructure cost by 30% without hurting reliability. What is your approach?
sym: Finance target: cut cloud spend 30% in a quarter. SLOs must stay green.
inv: # find the big spenders and waste
kubectl top nodes; compare requests vs usage
# idle resources, old snapshots, unattached volumes
cause: Typical findings: over-provisioned instances, idle environments running 24/7, unattached storage, no commitments on baseline, and chatty cross-zone data transfer.
fix: # rightsize instances and requests with SLO guardrails
# schedule non-prod shutdown nights/weekends
# savings plans for baseline, spot for tolerant batch
# delete orphaned volumes/snapshots, lifecycle storage
# reduce cross-AZ and egress traffic
prev: FinOps practice: tagging, showback, unit cost metrics, budgets, and regular reviews with engineers.
tip: Remove waste first, then optimise. Cutting capacity that is actually used trades money for incidents.
a: I start with visibility: break down spending by service, team and environment using tags, and measure utilisation to find waste. The first wave of savings is usually safe: shut down idle or non-production environments outside working hours, delete orphaned volumes, old snapshots and unused load balancers, and apply storage lifecycle rules. The second wave is rightsizing, reducing instance sizes and Kubernetes requests based on observed usage, with headroom and SLO monitoring as guardrails, and applying changes gradually. The third is purchasing strategy: commit to savings plans or reservations for steady baseline load and use spot capacity for fault-tolerant batch work. I also look at architecture-driven costs like cross-zone traffic, egress and over-retained logs. Throughout, I track unit costs such as cost per request, keep reliability metrics visible, and make sure engineers see their own spend, so savings last.
f: What should you cut first?
How do you protect reliability while cutting?
